english: Prana is the vital life force that animates all of creation; in the body it governs every function from breathing to thought. Pranayama is not merely breath control but the expansion and regulation of this life force. The breath is the most accessible handle on prana — by refining the breath we influence the mind, energy and health.
context: From Prana and Pranayama (Swami Niranjanananda). Foundational concept: mind and prana are intimately linked, so steadying the breath steadies the mind. Approach pranayama as working with energy, not just lungs.

english: Prana functions through five sub-pranas (vayus): prana vayu (chest — intake and inspiration), apana vayu (below the navel — elimination and downward flow), samana vayu (navel — digestion and balance), udana vayu (throat and head — upward movement, speech, expression) and vyana vayu (whole body — circulation and coordination). Pranayama harmonises these currents.
context: From Prana and Pranayama. Many techniques target a vayu: kapalbhati and agnisar stimulate samana/apana; ujjayi and bhramari soothe udana. Balancing prana (in) and apana (out) is a central aim.

english: Nadis are subtle channels through which prana flows. Three are central: ida nadi (terminating at the left nostril — lunar, cooling, associated with mental and passive energy), pingala nadi (right nostril — solar, heating, vital and active energy) and sushumna (the central channel up the spine, the path of spiritual awakening). Alternate nostril breathing balances ida and pingala so prana can enter sushumna.
context: From Prana and Pranayama. This is why nadi shodhana ('nadi purification') is the cornerstone practice — it balances the solar and lunar flows. Which nostril is dominant shifts through the day and reflects one's state.

english: The being is described as five sheaths (koshas): annamaya (physical/food body), pranamaya (energy body, reached through breath), manomaya (mental/emotional body), vijnanamaya (wisdom/intuitive body) and anandamaya (bliss body). Pranayama works directly on the pranamaya kosha, the bridge between body and mind.
context: From Prana and Pranayama. Explains why breathwork affects mood and clarity, not just the body: refining the energy sheath influences the mental sheath layered upon it.

english: Chakras are junctions where nadis converge, each linked to psychological and physical qualities: mooladhara (base/stability), swadhisthana (sacrum/emotion), manipura (navel/willpower and digestion), anahata (heart/compassion), vishuddhi (throat/expression), ajna (brow/insight) and sahasrara (crown). Pranayama and awareness direct prana to awaken and balance these centres.
context: From Prana and Pranayama. Useful for intention-setting: manipura for energy and confidence, anahata for emotional balance, ajna for focus and meditation.

english: Practise pranayama on an empty stomach, ideally at dawn or dusk, in a clean, airy, quiet place. Sit in a steady, comfortable meditation posture (sukhasana, padmasana, siddhasana or, if needed, vajrasana or a chair) with the spine erect and body relaxed. Breathe through the nose unless a technique says otherwise, and keep the face and shoulders soft.
context: From Asana Pranayama Mudra Bandha (Swami Satyananda). Good posture and an empty stomach prevent strain. Beginners should master steady sitting and full yogic breathing before formal pranayama.

english: Nasagra (nasikagra) mudra is the hand position used to control the nostrils in alternate-nostril practices. Fold the index and middle fingers of the right hand into the palm; use the thumb to close the right nostril and the ring finger to close the left. Keep the hand light and the elbow relaxed, not lifting the shoulder.
context: From APMB. Used in nadi shodhana, surya bhedana and chandra bhedana. Some traditions extend the index/middle fingers to the eyebrow centre (Vishnu mudra variant).

english: Begin with simple breath awareness: sit quietly and observe the natural breath at the nostrils without changing it, feeling it cool on inhalation and warm on exhalation. This settles the mind, reveals the breathing pattern, and is the essential first practice before any technique.
context: From APMB. Safe for everyone and a complete practice in itself for calming anxiety. Recommended 5–10 minutes daily as the foundation of all breathwork.

english: Abdominal (diaphragmatic) breathing uses the diaphragm: on inhalation the abdomen gently expands, on exhalation it draws in, while the chest stays relatively still. It is the most efficient, relaxing way to breathe and reverses the shallow chest breathing of stress.
context: From APMB. Practise lying or seated with a hand on the belly. The base of full yogic breathing; deeply calming and safe for all, including for lowering anxiety before sleep.

english: The full yogic breath combines abdominal, thoracic and clavicular breathing into one smooth wave: inhalation fills the belly, then the ribcage, then the upper chest; exhalation releases in reverse, upper chest, ribs, then belly. It maximises oxygenation and is the platform for advanced pranayama.
context: From APMB. Master this before adding ratios, retention or fast breathing. Practise slowly without strain; a few minutes daily builds capacity and calm.

english: Nadi shodhana (alternate nostril breathing) purifies and balances the ida and pingala nadis. Using nasagra mudra, breathe in through the left nostril, then out through the right; in through the right, out through the left — that is one round. It is taught in graded stages, first equal inhalation and exhalation, later adding retention and a controlled ratio.
context: From APMB. The single most important, universally beneficial pranayama: calms the mind, balances the nervous system and prepares for meditation. Beginners keep it smooth without retention; the classic refined ratio of inhale:retention:exhale is 1:4:2, approached only gradually. Avoid forced retention with high blood pressure or heart conditions.

english: Ujjayi ('victorious breath') is performed by gently contracting the glottis at the back of the throat so the breath makes a soft oceanic sound, while breathing slowly through the nose. It lengthens and smooths the breath and turns attention inward.
context: From APMB. Calming and safe; can be practised seated, lying down, or combined with other techniques and asana. Excellent for insomnia, anxiety and slowing a racing mind. Keep the sound soft, never straining the throat.

english: Bhramari (humming bee breath) uses a long, smooth exhalation with a steady humming sound like a bee, the inhalation being normal. Optionally the ears are closed with the thumbs (shanmukhi) to internalise the sound. The vibration soothes the nervous system.
context: From APMB. Powerfully relieves stress, anger, anxiety and insomnia and lowers blood pressure. Safe for most; avoid lying down while humming and skip during acute ear infection. Practise 5–10 rounds.

english: Sheetali is a cooling pranayama: roll the tongue into a tube, inhale slowly through the rolled tongue, withdraw the tongue and exhale through the nose. It cools the body, quenches thirst and calms hunger and irritability.
context: From APMB. Best in heat or for excess pitta (heat, acidity, anger). Avoid in cold weather, with low blood pressure, respiratory conditions like asthma/bronchitis, or excessive mucus. If the tongue cannot roll, use sitkari.

english: Sitkari is a cooling breath done by gently clenching the teeth, drawing the lips back and inhaling with a hissing sound across the teeth, then exhaling through the nose. Like sheetali it cools and calms, and suits those who cannot roll the tongue.
context: From APMB. Same cooling benefits and cautions as sheetali: avoid in cold weather, low blood pressure and respiratory disorders, and with sensitive teeth or gums.

english: Kapalbhati ('skull shining') is a cleansing technique of short, forceful exhalations by sharply contracting the abdomen, with passive, automatic inhalations. It clears the lungs and sinuses, energises the mind and tones the abdominal organs.
context: From APMB. This is stimulating, not calming — practise in the morning, not before sleep. Start with 3 rounds of ~20 strokes at a comfortable pace. CONTRAINDICATED in high blood pressure, heart disease, stroke, hernia, epilepsy, vertigo, during pregnancy or menstruation, and with abdominal surgery or ulcers. Stop if dizzy.

english: Bhastrika ('bellows breath') uses forceful and equal inhalation and exhalation from the abdomen and chest, like a blacksmith's bellows, generating heat and vitality. It is done in rounds, often followed by a slow breath and retention.
context: From APMB. Strongly heating and energising; builds prana and clears the nadis. CONTRAINDICATED in high blood pressure, heart disease, hernia, epilepsy, and during pregnancy. Learn under guidance; keep the pace controlled and stop at any dizziness.

english: Surya bhedana ('piercing the sun') activates pingala, the solar/heating channel: inhale always through the right nostril and exhale through the left, using nasagra mudra, optionally with retention. It raises energy, warmth and alertness.
context: From APMB. Use for low energy, sluggishness or cold; practise earlier in the day, not near sleep. Avoid with high blood pressure, heart disease, hyperacidity, epilepsy or anxiety/overstimulation. Its opposite, chandra bhedana, cools.

english: Chandra bhedana ('piercing the moon') activates ida, the lunar/cooling channel: inhale always through the left nostril and exhale through the right. It cools, calms and quietens mental activity.
context: From APMB. Use for heat, stress, anger or trouble winding down at night. Avoid with low blood pressure, depression or heavy mucus/cold. The mirror of surya bhedana.

english: Kumbhaka is the retention of breath — antar kumbhaka (holding after inhalation) and bahir kumbhaka (holding after exhalation). Retention is the heart of classical pranayama, deepening the effect on prana, but it is introduced only after the breath is long, smooth and effortless, and always without strain.
context: From Prana and Pranayama. Never force or grip; the throat, face and heart stay relaxed. Classic ratios such as inhale:hold:exhale 1:4:2 are goals reached over months, not starting points. Skip retention entirely with high blood pressure, heart conditions, or during pregnancy.

english: Bandhas are energetic 'locks' used with pranayama to direct prana: jalandhara bandha (throat lock — chin drawn toward the chest), moola bandha (contraction of the perineum) and uddiyana bandha (drawing the abdomen up and in, done only on external retention). Combined they form maha bandha.
context: From APMB. Bandhas intensify retention practices and awaken sushumna, but are advanced. Uddiyana and forceful bandhas are contraindicated in high blood pressure, heart disease, ulcers, hernia, and during pregnancy or menstruation. Learn from a teacher.

english: Moorchha is an advanced, meditative pranayama combining slow inhalation, jalandhara bandha and long retention with the awareness turned upward, producing a swooning, deeply internal calm. It is practised only after mastery of retention and bandhas.
context: From APMB. Not for beginners. Contraindicated in high blood pressure, heart disease, epilepsy, vertigo and any brain condition. Included here for reference — recommend foundational practices instead unless the practitioner is experienced and supervised.

english: Pranayama is powerful and must be practised safely. Gentle practices — breath awareness, abdominal and full yogic breathing, nadi shodhana without retention, ujjayi and bhramari — are safe for almost everyone. Forceful or retention practices — kapalbhati, bhastrika, surya bhedana, strong kumbhaka and bandhas — are contraindicated in high or unstable blood pressure, heart disease, stroke, epilepsy, hernia, ulcers, glaucoma, recent surgery, and during pregnancy.
context: From APMB and Prana and Pranayama. Always stop at dizziness, breathlessness or discomfort; never strain; progress gradually; and learn advanced techniques under a qualified teacher. When in doubt, choose the gentle practices.

english: The tradition teaches a strict order: first steady sitting and breath awareness, then abdominal and full yogic breathing, then nadi shodhana and gentle techniques, and only later — once the breath is long and effortless — retention (kumbhaka), ratios and bandhas. Each stage is stabilised before the next is added.
context: From APMB. Rushing to retention or fast breathing causes strain and harm. A good rule: if the breath is not smooth and silent, you are not ready for the next stage. Consistency of a short daily practice beats occasional long sessions.
